records.note: Reception of the forecaster's own newsletter repost ('will be a hit' with newer subscribers): not a regulatory, trial, company, payer or practice outcome. Readers, not the author, decide reception, so CONTROL does not fit; but 'a hit' has no benchmark, series or resolution source either (VAGUE would also fail). 'Today' is a time word, but nothing resolvable attaches to it. 'Will be' would be bin A if there were an event.

The newsletter's own upcoming topics (including 'why I use my middle name online'): the forecaster's own publication decides what it publishes, so the outcome is in his control. 'Doubtless breathtaking' is self-mocking, the list includes a joke topic (private equity in teen paranormal romance), and the text is recycled from an earlier publication. Also outside the five areas. CONTROL is the primary failing test.

Restates a published JAMA Health Forum case-control finding (roughly 20 percent higher odds of billing from another practice within two years of a private equity sale) as a standing rule. Information about a completed study, not an expectation: no acquisition, practice set, series or period is named, and 'in the next two years' is the study's follow-up window, not a date. Read as a forecast it would still fail as VAGUE (no countable set, no series). 'Highly likely' would be bin B.

'A lot of these private equity roll ups' is a quantifier with no countable set; 'end up becoming part of Optum' names no target practice or roll-up, no series, no threshold and no deadline. A company_event needs a named company or program and a definitive announcement; nothing can be written without inventing the set. 'Likely' would be bin B. Optum and UnitedHealth Group are not in the forecaster's affiliation list.

'They' (physician practices bought by private equity) has no countable set, 'a company like Optum' names no acquirer, and 'bankrupted or acquired' has no series, threshold or deadline. The 'either ... or' would be one event by rule, but there is no asset to write it on. Largely a present-tense description of a pattern ('They're getting bought') with no confidence phrase. Restates the owen-1615 call.

Clinical prognosis for one family member's child with ADHD ('most likely to do great'): not a regulatory, trial, company, payer or practice outcome. Also no benchmark for 'do great' and no resolution source. 'Most likely' would be bin B. Restated at owen-1631 and owen-1633.

'More effective treatment coming' is a quantifier ('more') and a comparative ('more effective') with no countable set or benchmark; 'coming' and 'in the future' are not deadlines. The named candidates (low-dose LSD for ADHD, TMS for ADHD, transcranial focused ultrasound, fMRI-EEG neurofeedback) are listed as pipeline examples with no outcome type: the forecaster does not say approval, trial result or market availability, and closes with 'I don't actually know'. Writing an approval or trial event for any candidate would invent the outcome type and the deadline, so no -a/-b split is possible. The confidence words (absolutely, probably, maybe, may, likely) attach to different candidates.

Developmental prognosis for one child ('going to grow out of a lot of these symptoms'): outside the five areas. Also 'a lot of these symptoms' has no threshold, there is no resolution source, and 'as your kid gets older' is not a deadline. 'Going to' would be bin A.

'The rock-solid causality answer' on long-term ADHD treatment has no benchmark, and no trial, sponsor, registry entry or publication is named; the claim is that an unethical long-term randomized trial will never exist. No entity or observable event can be written. 'Never gonna' would be bin E with asserts false, but there is no event to deny, and 'never' sets no deadline.

A claim about the therapist a hypothetical Talkspace user would be matched with (one trained in organizational skills training): no public series, benchmark or resolution source exists for one user's match, and the claim is really a present-state description of Talkspace's therapist pool. Not a company or market outcome as the templates define one. 'Highly skeptical' would be bin D. Talkspace is not in the forecaster's affiliation list.

'The next generation of treatments' has no countable set; 'better efficacy and a lower side effect profile' is a comparative with no named trial, endpoint, comparator or effect-size threshold, and no deadline. 'Promise' is not a lexicon phrase. The Mind Medicine LSD trials, TMS and the Monarch eTNS device are context, not the asset of the claim sentence. Nothing can be written without inventing a trial and a benchmark.

Present-tense description ('is in the process of being developed') from a 2013 alpha-agonist review. The author adopts the text ('For me, in 2023, the above still holds'), so it is his own adopted statement rather than THIRD_PARTY; but it states information about a development program, not an expectation of a future state, and names no sponsor, trial, filing or deadline. Recycled text: the endorsement says 2023 in a 2025 post.

'Novel treatments ... they're coming' has no countable set, no named asset, no outcome type and no deadline ('coming' is on the not-a-deadline list). Restates the owen-1618 call; the sentence begins 'For me, in 2023', so the text is recycled. 'Coming' would be bin A ('is coming'), but there is no event.

Mortality prognosis for one child if ADHD is left untreated, drawn from Swedish registry data: not a regulatory, trial, company, payer or practice outcome. Also a comparative risk ('more likely ... earlier') with no benchmark or resolution source. 'More likely' would be bin B. Compare owen-1626, which restates the same epidemiology as data.

Restates a BMJ life-expectancy finding (7 to 9 fewer years for adults with ADHD) as 'early death at 68, not 76' and asserts the causes are preventable: information about published data plus a present-tense evaluative claim, not an expectation of a future event. The condition 'if people don't take care of themselves' is not observable. Also outside the five areas (compare owen-1625).

'I try mine tonight': the forecaster's own action with his own Monarch eTNS device; he alone decides whether it happens. Also outside the five areas and of no forecast value. The post discloses that Fermata (co-founder) offers the device, but the sentence is a personal plan, not a claim about the device.

'A revolution in ADHD for kids' and 'the Neuro-modulated future of our field' are slogans: no entity, series, threshold or countable set for Monarch eTNS adoption, no confidence phrase, and 'future' is not a deadline. Practice-adoption area guess, but nothing can be written without inventing a series. The forecaster discloses that Fermata (co-founder) offers the device; the affiliated tag would apply if an event existed.

Conditional practice claim: 'if physicians prescribe this medical device ... they may avoid stimulants in many cases'. 'Many cases' is a quantifier with no countable set, no series (prescription or claims data) and no threshold; the condition (physicians prescribing Monarch eTNS) has no defined set either, and there is no deadline. 'May' would be bin C. Fermata (co-founder) offers the device, per the post.

'We don't solve ADHD at scale by doing things that aren't scalable' is a slogan: no entity, observable event, series, threshold or deadline. 'I don't think' would be a bin D reading, but there is no proposition to deny. Practice-adoption area guess only; the stimulant-supply and DEA context does not enter the claim sentence.

Restatement of the owen-1617 prognosis for one child ('gonna be OK ... the most likely outcome'): outside the five areas, no benchmark, no resolution source. 'Most likely' would be bin B. Not DUPLICATE: a different sentence in a different section, not a double capture of one row.

Medication-response prognosis for one child ('that stimulant is probably gonna work'): outside the five areas; no benchmark, no resolution source, and the passage allows dose, formulation or combination changes, so the proposition has no fixed form. 'Probably' would be bin B.

Third restatement of the prognosis for one child ('the treatment is highly likely to help'), with a condition ('if you stick with it') that the family controls: outside the five areas, no benchmark, no resolution source. 'Highly likely' would be bin B.

'Value based contracts take years of careful pruning' is a general timing claim about payer contracting with no named payer, contract, series or threshold; 'years' attaches to no event and no date, and there is no confidence phrase. Drawn from the forecaster's own UnitedHealth Group negotiations for his own companies, so a specific reading would also be CONTROL. Payer area guess, but nothing can be written without inventing a contract.

'I'm not saying it's going to get you a contract' is a disclaimer of a prediction: no future state is asserted, and no payer, provider, contract or deadline is named. A hedged caveat, not a denial with a proposition (asserts false would need an event).

'The best predictor of a pilot turning into a contract ... is the stability of leadership in the company' is a general heuristic from the forecaster's past pilots: a descriptive correlation, not an asserted future state; no pilot, payer, series or deadline. Read as a forecast it would also fail as VAGUE.

The forecaster's own memoir in progress ('It's gonna be exciting. In theory.'): the reception of a book is outside the five areas, 'exciting' has no benchmark, and the self-hedge 'In theory' undercuts the assertion. Whether the book appears is his own decision (CONTROL), but the sentence claims quality, which readers judge, so OUT_OF_AREA is the primary failing test.

'I'm gonna get back to that' (an article about a research study): the newsletter's own programming, decided by the forecaster. Also outside the five areas. The rest of the post is a satirical song in an imagined voice (Vivek Ramaswamy on DOGE) and carries no sincere forecast.

'More is coming' (further lesion-network targets for other disorders): 'more' is a quantifier with no countable set, no named disorder, research group, publication or series, and 'coming' is not a deadline. 'Is coming' would be bin A, but there is no event. The Fox and Siddiqi groups are context, not the forecaster's organizations.

'A more effective discipline to emerge' is a comparative with no benchmark, series, threshold or deadline; 'these two lines of evidence' (connectome-based targeting; iTBS plus d-cycloserine) are inputs, not an asset with an outcome type. 'I think ... will' would be bin B. Practice-adoption guess only.

'Game changing OCD treatment' is a slogan, and 'would be' is an evaluative counterfactual about iTBS alone, not a claim that a named body or series will do something by a date. The McGirr et al. 2025 trial result the sentence comments on is already published, so a trial reading would be KNOWN. The post discloses that Fermata (co-founder) and Ampa Health (trial site) offer the treatment, so an adoption event would be CONTROL or affiliated; but there is no event to write.

The antecedent ('a cure for depression, tomorrow, that worked 100% of the time') is a counterfactual that cannot be observed, so the conditional rule does not apply; 'get it paid for' names no payer, program, code or coverage policy; 'I'm still not sure' is not a lexicon phrase. 'In a decade' would set 2035-03-10 by the anchor table, but there is no event to attach it to. The claim applies to psychedelic medicine only by context.

'More appropriate payment for transcranial magnetic stimulation' is a comparative with no benchmark (no payer, code, fee schedule or rate named), and 'a long way to go' has no threshold or deadline. Mostly a present-tense assessment of the forecaster's own advocacy. Payer area guess, but nothing can be written without inventing a payer and a rate.

The forecaster hosts the next RAMHT (Rapid-Acting Mental Health Treatment) conference, which he organizes: his own organization's event on a date it sets (May 18, 2025, Los Angeles). Own-venture commitment, never scored. Also outside the five areas.

Fruit snacks at Fruit Logistica trade-fair events: outside the five areas, and 'several of these events' has no countable set or resolution source. Joke framing in a humorous essay about a name clash between Fermata and an agtech company. 'I have to believe there will be' would read as bin A if there were an event.

The forecaster's own possible attendance at Fruit Logistica in Berlin ('I might have to drop into Berlin'): his own decision, self-conditioned on being free. Also outside the five areas. 'Next February' would set 2026-02-28 by the anchor table, but a personal plan is never scored.

'Additional investigations ... for other conduct ... in other places' names no case, court, agency or docket, and 'may meet the level of criminal or civil liability' describes the legal character of conduct, not a verdict, sentence, judgment or filed settlement in a named case as the court_outcome template requires. No deadline. Writing an event would invent the case set and the outcome type. 'May' would be bin C. UnitedHealth Group is not in the forecaster's affiliation list.

Publication timing for the tardive dyskinesia video-screening algorithm the forecaster built with Anthony Sterns (iRxReminder, where he was Chief Medical Officer in 2024) and Videra Health (strategic advisor; TDscreen is an alias): the forecaster's own organizations control the submission and the release of results. 'Shortly' is not a deadline in any case. The performance claim ('better than any human study') reports an unpublished result and is not a forecast.

Personal health plan and a hedged expectation that the new tardive dyskinesia medications (tetrabenazine, valbenazine) may help the forecaster himself: outside the five areas, one patient, no resolution source. Seeing a movement disorders doctor is his own decision. 'Maybe ... will be' would be bin C.

'I will probably write about it' in his own newsletter: the forecaster's own publication decides. Also outside the five areas. 'Will probably' would be bin B, but own-venture commitments are never scored.

Present-tense property claims about Cobenfy: 'the very first novel antipsychotic that doesn't cause weight gain', 'doesn't cause movement disorders', 'available for people with psychosis now'. Descriptive, with no future state, deciding body, series or deadline. The finder's implicit long-term reading (no movement disorders will emerge) is not in the forecaster's words.
